name: ǁAni
confidence_why: ǁAni is a tone language on every account (Vossen 2003; WALS after Vossen 1986 and 1997; Downing 2004), and the two field descriptions of its verbal stress, Heine 1999 and Vossen 2003, both put it on the last high-toned syllable of the verb and differ only in detail (Heine's preceding-low-tone condition and his doubt about its significance; Vossen's finding that it is inherent to tone classes 2, 3 and 5 and shifts to the juncture morpheme in classes 1 and 4), so the record rests on few sources but faces no real dissent.

In Rose-Juliet Anyanwu (ed.), Stress and Tone – the African Experience (Frankfurter Afrikanistische Blätter 15), 181-191. Köln: Rüdiger Köppe. [quoting Heine, Bernd. 1999. (Google Books GData feed, vols. iyMOAQAAMAAJ / AZGUEQmFqfMC / emVnZA8KPQwC)
catalog_quote: [Vossen 2003: 181-182, §1] Stress is said to exist but, according to Heine, its "exact significance is unclear." ... stress appears to play a certain role in the formation of finite verbs. Heine (1999: 18) cautiously states: "Typically it is found on the last high tone syllable preceded by a low tone within the same word." My own data, however, seem to suggest that stress as a distinctive unit is inherent even to the citation form of the verb. This article is strictly empirical-descriptive. It confines itself to the treatment of verbal tone and stress ... [pp. 185-186, §5 The interaction of tone and stress] Besides tone, stress appears to play an important role in the formation of finite verbs. In most cases it is acoustically perceptible. To verbs of tone classes 2, 3 and 5 stress is inherent in the sense that the accent is retained on the verbal stem throughout, be it simple, derived, reduplicated or composed. In each case the stress-bearing unit is the last H-tone syllable. ... verbs of tone classes 1 and 4 are observed to shift stress to the juncture morpheme. [Downing 2010: 394] Vossen (2003) shows that in ǁAni (Central Khoisan) stress is assigned to the last High-toned syllable of verbs. As all lexical morphemes have at least one High tone, all lexical morphemes appear to be assigned stress. [fn.] ... including some exceptions to the pattern mentioned here.
sweep_summary: ǁAni is not in the catalog. Both works with stress in the title are the same work, Vossen 2003 'Verbal tone and stress in ǁAni' (FAB 15:181-191), which is the only first-hand treatment of ǁAni stress; no open copy exists (Köppe print; HathiTrust/Frankfurt/De Gruyter routes blocked), but Google Books feed snippets now yield section 5 almost verbatim: stress sits on the last H-toned syllable of the verb stem for tone classes 2/3/5 and shifts to the juncture morpheme for classes 1/4, with the intro quoting Heine 1999:18 ('last high tone syllable preceded by a low tone within the same word'). Downing 2010 (paywalled, p. 394) summarises this as 'last High-toned syllable of verbs' with exceptions; Downing 2004 (open, read) predates it and has nothing on ǁAni. Heine 1999 (Khoisan Forum 11) remains print-only. A catalog entry would be coded from Vossen 2003 as tone-conditioned, verb-only stress (last H syllable of stem, or juncture); acquiring the full Vossen article (and Heine 1999) is the high-priority gap.

new_statements.rule_in_words: ǁAni is a (mora-based) tone language; in addition, verbs carry a stress whose position is tied to tone: it falls on the last High-toned syllable of the word (Heine: the last H syllable preceded by a L within the word). Vossen argues stress is a distinctive property already of the verb's citation form (he marks it lexically per verb stem in an appendix), and Downing notes Vossen reports exceptions to the last-H generalisation.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing seen in the accessible snippets.
new_statements.exceptions: Downing 2010 fn.: 'See Vossen (2003) for detailed discussion of ǁAni, including some exceptions to the pattern mentioned here.' Vossen: homophonous citation forms can differ in finite shapes; stress treated as distinctive (lexical) in verbs.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about verbs (citation forms and finite verb forms incl. juncture/TAM suffixes); nominal stress not treated by Vossen 2003 ('confines itself to the treatment of verbal tone and stress'). Word-level, tone-conditioned.
new_statements.identity_note: All statements concern ǁAni proper (anii1246; Vossen's fieldwork on the upper Okavango, Ngamiland; Heine 1999 same variety). Fehn 2019 treats ǁAni as a variety of the Khwe dialect cluster (Khwe = kxoe1243, separate languoid); Kilian-Hatz 2008 describes West Caprivi Khwe, not ǁAni. Fehn's open Ts'ixa grammar describes Ts'ixa (own Glottolog languoid, though 'Ts'éxa' appears among Glottolog's //Ani alt names) and was not used for the statement.

new_statements.reading: ǁAni verbs carry a tone-dependent stress: in tone classes 2, 3 and 5 the stress stays on the last high-toned syllable of the verb stem in all forms; in tone classes 1 and 4 it moves to the juncture (tense) morpheme in finite forms, so stress placement is lexically conditioned by tone class and morphologically conditioned by the juncture, not a fixed edge-based rule. Nouns are not treated. Caveat: assembled from overlapping snippet views, not from a full copy; the passage boundaries are exact but a few words between 'listed in (9)' and 'verbs of tone classes 1 and 4' are missing.

tone_statements.quote: ǁAni distinguishes three tone levels H(igh), M(id) and L(ow), which may be combined into two level (HH, MM) and four contour melodies (MH, HM, ML, HL) (Fehn 2019). Like in related Kalahari Khoe languages (see Fehn 2016 on Ts’ixa, 2019 on Khwe), the tone-bearing unit in ǁAni is the mora, rather than the syllable. Inherited lexical roots consistently display two morae, while grammatical elements may be monomoraic. As already implied in Fehn (2019: 24), speakers of ǁAni differ in the tonal realization of certain lexemes, depending on the underlying proto-tone pattern (cf. Elderkin 2004, 2013).

readall_conflicts: No new conflict. Downing 2004 (p. 111) says she could find no discussion of stress in the Khoisan literature, whereas the catalog's Vossen 2003 (FAB 15:181-191) describes stress in ǁAni verbs; this is a matter of date, not a disagreement about the language, and Downing's 2010 chapter (snippet, p. 394) cites Vossen 2003 and repeats his rule (stress on the last High-toned syllable of verbs). Within the existing statements there is a mild tension already on record: Heine 1999:18 (as quoted by Vossen) calls the significance of stress 'unclear' and puts it 'typically' on the last high-tone syllable preceded by a low tone, while Vossen 2003 treats stress as inherent to verbs of tone classes 2, 3 and 5 (last H syllable of the stem) and shifted to the juncture morpheme in classes 1 and 4.
